findings: Brief runs of asymptomatic sinus tachycardia. No sustained arrhythmia, no pauses greater than 2 seconds, no AV block.
cardiac_monitoring.impression: Sinus rhythm with brief runs of asymptomatic sinus tachycardia (maximum 122 bpm). No arrhythmia, pause or AV block.
cardiac_monitoring.rhythm_summary: Predominant sinus rhythm throughout the recording

csf.interpretation: Unremarkable CSF. Normal cell count, protein, and glucose.

ct.impression: No acute intracranial abnormality. No haemorrhage, mass, hydrocephalus, or large-territory infarct.

findings: Normal sinus rhythm. Normal axis and intervals. No acute ST-T changes.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Left Hoover sign, distractible arm weakness and dragging gait; midline sensory split supportive only
action_criteria.label: Examine for positive functional signs
action_criteria.rationale: The left hemiparesis is diagnosed at the bedside: the Hoover sign, distractibility and a dragging gait are signs of clinical incompatibility (DSM-5 criterion B; McWhirter 2011; Daum 2014).

action_criteria.expected_evidence: No acute infarct on DWI and no lesion in the right motor pathway
action_criteria.label: Non-contrast brain MRI, once
action_criteria.rationale: A sudden left hemiparesis in a young woman is triaged as a possible stroke, including dissection; one non-contrast MRI with DWI answers that question, and gadolinium adds nothing (Espay 2018).

action_criteria.label: Review the medication list
action_criteria.rationale: Escitalopram alone carries no interaction that bears on the presentation; the review is defensible but not needed.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Quantifies mood, anxiety and symptom burden to guide therapy; does not make the diagnosis
action_criteria.label: Neuropsychological assessment of the comorbidity
action_criteria.rationale: Social anxiety disorder and the past anorexia nervosa are treatment context; a battery can quantify them but does not make the diagnosis (Espay 2018).

action_criteria.expected_evidence: General evidence on positive signs and treatment trials in FND
action_criteria.label: Search the literature on FND diagnosis and treatment
action_criteria.rationale: Background reading only; the diagnosis and the plan rest on this patient's examination and recorded data, not on a search.

prohibited_recommendations: Order further investigations once the positive diagnosis is established, without a new specific clinical question (repeat MRI, CT, lumbar puncture, EMG or nerve conduction studies, evoked potentials, PET).
Tell the patient the symptoms are imagined, feigned, 'all in your head', or that nothing is wrong.
Perform invasive testing without a specific indication (lumbar puncture, nerve or muscle biopsy, catheter angiography).
Give gadolinium contrast without a specific indication.
required_recommendations: Make a positive diagnosis of functional neurological disorder (functional limb weakness, left hemiparesis) based on the left Hoover sign, distractibility of the arm weakness and the dragging monoplegic gait, and not by exclusion of other disease.

Explain the diagnosis to the patient, and with consent to the family, as a common and genuine disorder of nervous system functioning that can improve, show the positive signs, and give written information.
Refer for physiotherapy with expertise in functional motor disorder (motor retraining, Nielsen 2015 consensus).
Refer for psychological therapy by a clinician experienced in FND (CBT-informed) and treat the comorbid social anxiety disorder.

avoided_actions.rationale: She went pale at onset but did not lose consciousness, and the deficit has positive functional signs; the mild tachycardia of a distressed patient raises no cardiac question.
There are no episodes of loss of consciousness and no embolic question once the MRI shows no infarct; rhythm monitoring answers nothing.
Two days after onset, with no thrombolysis decision pending, the single MRI with DWI answers the stroke question and a CT adds radiation without adding information.
No headache, fever, meningism or encephalopathy; a lumbar puncture is invasive and answers no question.
PET has no role in functional weakness.
A hemiparesis with normal reflexes and positive functional signs is not a neuromuscular question; a normal study reinforces the search for an organic cause.
Sensory loss stopping exactly at the midline is not a somatosensory pathway question; evoked potentials add nothing.

accepted: Functional neurological disorder — functional left hemiparesis

differential.diagnosis: Acute ischemic stroke (including cervical artery dissection) or TIA
differential.key_features: A sudden left hemiparesis in a young woman raises stroke or dissection, but face and tongue are spared, the Hoover sign and distractibility are positive, reflexes are normal and the MRI shows no restricted diffusion.

key_clinical_evidence: Positive signs of functional weakness on the left: Hoover sign, arm strength improving from 2/5 to 4/5 with distraction, and a dragging monoplegic gait; sensory loss stopping at the midline and normal walking when unobserved are supportive only.

Face and tongue are spared and reflexes are normal and symmetric two days after onset, so no upper motor neuron sign accompanies the dense arm weakness; this is supportive but does not by itself exclude a brain lesion.
A single non-contrast MRI with DWI, indicated by a sudden hemiparesis in a young woman, shows no infarct or other lesion.
Onset immediately after the dissertation rejection, the visa pressure and her social anxiety are context and a treatment target; a stressor is neither required nor sufficient for the diagnosis.

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Psychiatric history neither establishes nor refutes FND; the diagnosis rests on the positive signs, and the anxiety is a treatment target.
red_herrings.data_point: Social anxiety disorder on escitalopram and past anorexia nervosa
red_herrings.intended_effect: Anchoring on a 'psychosomatic' label without eliciting positive signs, or dismissing the symptoms as anxiety

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: A stressor is supportive context only; sudden hemiparesis still earns one MRI, and the positive signs make the diagnosis.
red_herrings.data_point: Onset immediately after the call rejecting her dissertation proposal, with her visa at stake
red_herrings.intended_effect: Concluding that stress 'caused' the weakness and skipping the examination and the stroke question

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: There was no loss of consciousness and the tachycardia fits her distress; with positive signs and no infarct there is no cardiac question.
red_herrings.data_point: Went pale and dropped the phone at onset; heart rate 104
red_herrings.intended_effect: Pursuing a cardiac or embolic cause with ECG, rhythm monitoring or echocardiography

sequence_constraints.reason: The examination comes first: its positive signs decide whether imaging has a specific question to answer (Espay 2018).

findings.result: Left hip extension weak on direct testing, full strength during contralateral right hip flexion against resistance.
Left arm strength improves from 2/5 to 4/5 while she performs an arithmetic task.
Left leg dragged behind without foot drop.
Left-sided loss to all sensory modalities stopping exactly at the midline; normal walking in the hallway when unaware of being observed; not counted as rule-in signs.
Reflexes normal and symmetric; no pathological reflexes.

clinical_assessment.impression: Positive signs of functional weakness: left Hoover sign, distractibility of left arm weakness and dragging monoplegic gait. The pattern is inconsistent with a structural lesion.

general.summary: No clinically significant interactions among the current medicines.

results.finding: Diagnosis of functional neurological disorder rests on positive clinical features such as the Hoover sign, tremor entrainment and functional seizure semiology, not on the exclusion of other disease; treatment combines explanation, physiotherapy and psychological therapy.
results.source: Espay AJ et al. JAMA Neurol 2018;75:1132-1141

results.finding: Motor signs such as the Hoover sign, hip abductor sign, drift without pronation and dragging gait have high specificity; sensory signs such as midline splitting have low specificity.
results.source: Daum C et al. J Neurol Neurosurg Psychiatry 2014;85:180-190

results.finding: Specialist physiotherapy for functional motor disorder was not superior to community neurological physiotherapy on physical function at 12 months; several secondary outcomes favoured it.
results.source: Nielsen G et al. Lancet Neurol 2024;23:675-686

results.finding: About 4% of patients diagnosed with conversion symptoms since 1970 later received another diagnosis.

functional neurological disorder diagnos.summary: Review and trial evidence supports a positive clinical diagnosis of functional neurological disorder from motor signs of high specificity, and physiotherapy whose effect on the trial's primary outcome was modest; a later revision of the diagnosis is uncommon.

additional_observations: Technique: sagittal T1, axial T2, axial FLAIR, DWI with ADC, SWI; no contrast administered
No restricted diffusion in any vascular territory
Normal internal capsule, corona radiata and motor cortex bilaterally
mri.impression: Normal non-contrast brain MRI. No acute infarct, white matter lesion, mass or hemorrhage.

metadata.difficulty_rationale: Clear positive signs of a functional left hemiparesis with a sudden onset that earns one MRI for the stroke question; cardiac tests, CT, nerve studies and evoked potentials are overuse.
metadata.notes: Straightforward FND: functional left hemiparesis in a PhD student; one non-contrast MRI with DWI answers the stroke-mimic question.
metadata.revision_reason: October 2026 review round: criteria rebuilt to the pack tiers (exam required, MRI recommended), non-contrast MRI, canonical literature and medication outputs, case-specific differential, evidence and assessment.

patient.chief_complaint: Sudden onset left-sided weakness following stressful phone call — 2 days duration

past_medical_history: Eating disorder history (anorexia, in remission 3 years)

social_history.recent_stressor: Dissertation proposal rejection by committee 3 weeks ago; visa status contingent on academic progress; family pressure from parents in Korea

patient.history_present_illness: Ms. J is a 26-year-old PhD student in biomedical engineering whose left arm and leg weakness began acutely approximately 2 days ago immediately following a phone call from her dissertation committee informing her that her proposal had been rejected and requiring major revisions. Her roommate witnessed the onset, describing that Ms. J went pale, dropped the phone, and immediately afterward could not use her left arm. She was brought to the emergency department. She is an international student on a student visa, and her immigration status depends on satisfactory academic progress; the dissertation rejection places her visa status under threat. Her parents in Korea are highly invested in her academic success. She has a history of anorexia nervosa currently in remission for 3 years and social anxiety disorder treated with escitalopram. She denies any headache at onset, loss of consciousness, or vision changes. She has had no prior neurological episodes. Her left-sided weakness has been stable over 2 days without deterioration. She is distressed but not showing la belle indifference.

neurological_exam.additional: No tongue or facial weakness. Speech normal.
neurological_exam.coordination: Normal right; cannot test left arm due to apparent weakness.
neurological_exam.gait: Left leg dragging without foot drop. Observed to walk normally in hallway when not aware of being observed.
neurological_exam.mental_status: Alert and oriented x4. Speaks quietly. Avoids eye contact. Highly anxious.
neurological_exam.motor: Left arm 2/5 on formal testing, improving to 4/5 when her attention is diverted by an arithmetic task. Left hip extension weak on direct testing; Hoover sign positive: left hip extension returns to full strength during contralateral right hip flexion against resistance. Right side 5/5.
neurological_exam.reflexes: Normal and symmetric. No pathological reflexes.
neurological_exam.sensory: Left-sided sensory loss to all modalities, abruptly stopping at the midline.
